attribution.note: Marcus states both clauses in his own voice.

semantics.note: The normalization preserves the ongoing trend and uncertainty about IP. It does not assert that OpenAI owns no IP.

contract.note: Increasing practical substitution is a fair ordinary reading of commoditization. Using 2022 reasonably frames the recent trend, though Marcus supplied neither that period nor a speed threshold. The qualified IP clause cannot establish an absence of IP.

evidence.note: The developers report GPT-3-comparable capabilities in 2022. This supports technical alternatives, but does not establish commercial substitution or its rate.
The original 2022 paper reports competitive benchmarks and model availability. Its tuning requirements and limited comparisons leave practical substitution uncertain.
OpenAI's dated disclosure establishes lower standard-model prices. It excludes fine-tuned models and does not establish comparable costs across suppliers.

Independent evaluation finds substantial improvement alongside performance gaps and adaptation barriers. These findings constrain substitution claims without establishing stagnation. Undisclosed methods do not establish exclusive, protectable IP.
Meta's release disclosure establishes noncommercial licensing and restricted access. These limits weaken OPT's relevance as a commercial substitute without disproving the broader trend.

reviews.rationale: Technical alternatives, improving open models and lower prices support the claimed direction. The packet does not establish rapid practical substitution across ordinary uses during 2022. Performance gaps, adaptation needs and access restrictions also do not establish stagnation. The IP clause expresses uncertainty and cannot be scored as a firm claim that no protectable advantage existed.
